title: Finite-height bounds and compatible rank-one coarsenings
statement: Let $K\subseteq L$ be fields [def-pc-field-extension], let $W\subseteq L$ be a valuation ring [def-trf-valuation-ring], and put $R=W\cap K$. Suppose $R$ has finite height $h$ and $\operatorname{trdeg}_K L=d<\infty$ [def-kun-transcendence-degree]. Height counts strict inclusions in chains of prime ideals. Then $W$ has finite height at most $h+d$. For any overring $W\subseteq A\subseteq L$, $A$ is a valuation ring, $\mathfrak m_A\subseteq W$, $W/\mathfrak m_A$ is a valuation ring of $A/\mathfrak m_A$, and $W$ is its inverse image under $A\to A/\mathfrak m_A$. Heights add under this composition. If $h>0$ and $(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}W=L$, then there is an overring $A\subset L$ of height one whose restriction $A\cap K=R_1$ has height one. Put $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak m_A$ and $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap K=\mathfrak m_{R_1}$. Then $R_0=R/\mathfrak p$ is a valuation ring of $k=R_1/\mathfrak p$ of height $h-1$, $W_0=W/\mathfrak q$ is a valuation ring of $E=A/\mathfrak q$, and $W_0\cap k=R_0$. The coarsened valuations on $K,L$ are compatible. For a subfield $F\subseteq L$ containing $K$, restriction to $F$ commutes with these inverse-image descriptions.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.4 and its preceding composition discussion, printed p. 8; finite-height bound from the relative Abhyankar inequality, Lemma 2.1.2, and the prime/convex-subgroup correspondence in section 2.1; the bounded coarsening used in the proof of Theorem 2.1.8, printed p. 13.

proof.text: Choose a transcendence basis $B$ of $L/K$ using [lem-exc-transcendence-basis-exists]. By [def-kun-transcendence-degree], $|B|=d$, and by [def-weil-pbc-transcendence-basis], $L$ is algebraic over $T=K(B)$. Put $U=W\cap T$. By [lem-trf-valuation-algebraic-height], contraction identifies the prime chains of $W$ and $U$. We may therefore prove the height bound for $U$ over $R=U\cap K$. Notice that $T/K$ is finitely generated, even though $L/K$ need not be.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.2 (relative inequality); finite-transcendence-degree reduction to a finite transcendence basis, using algebraic height invariance.

proof.text: Write $\Gamma=T^\times/U^\times$ and $H=K^\times/R^\times$. The inclusion embeds $H$ as an ordered subgroup of $\Gamma$: a ratio of elements of $K$ belongs to $U$ exactly when it belongs to $R$. Apply [lem-trf-abhyankar-inequality] to the finitely generated extension $T/K$: it gives $\operatorname{rrk}(\Gamma/H)\le d$, after discarding the nonnegative residue transcendence degree. The prime/convex correspondence [lem-trf-valuation-prime-convex-correspondence] for $R$ bounds all convex chains in $H$ by $h$. Thus [lem-trf-relative-convex-chain-bound] bounds convex chains in $\Gamma$ by $h+d$. Applying the same prime/convex correspondence to $U$ and then Step 1 proves the asserted height bound for $W$.

source.place: Section 2.1, prime/convex correspondence and Lemma 2.1.2; relative convex-chain estimate.

proof.text: For an arbitrary subring $W\subseteq A\subseteq L$, the alternative $x\in W$ or $x^{-1}\in W$ from [def-trf-valuation-ring] holds in $A$, so $A$ is a valuation ring. Let $\mathfrak q=\mathfrak m_A$. If $0\ne x\in\mathfrak q$ were outside $W$, then $x^{-1}\in W\subseteq A$, contradicting $x\in\mathfrak m_A$. Hence $\mathfrak q\subseteq W$. It is an ideal of $W$ as well as of $A$. For $\bar a\ne0$ in $A/\mathfrak q$, any lift $a$ is a unit of $A$, and $a$ or $a^{-1}$ lies in $W$. Consequently $W/\mathfrak q$ satisfies the valuation-ring alternative inside the field $A/\mathfrak q$. Finally, if $a\bmod\mathfrak q$ is the residue of $w\in W$, then $a-w\in\mathfrak q\subseteq W$, so $a\in W$. This proves the inverse-image assertion.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.4(i), with the element and residue-lift arguments expanded.

proof.text: By [lem-trf-valuation-overring-prime-localization], $A=W_{\mathfrak q}$: the corresponding prime is $\mathfrak q\cap W=\mathfrak q$ by Step 3. By [lem-weil-pbc-primes-of-localization], primes of $A$ identify with primes of $W$ contained in $\mathfrak q$. Primes of $W/\mathfrak q$ identify with primes of $W$ containing $\mathfrak q$: inverse image and quotient $P\mapsto P/\mathfrak q$ are inverse, inclusion-preserving maps, with primality checked by multiplying representatives. All ideals of $W$ are comparable: if $a\in I\setminus J$ is nonzero, then for $0\ne b\in J$ the alternative $a/b\in W$ would put $a\in J$, so $b/a\in W$ and $b\in I$; thus $J\subseteq I$. Hence every prime lies below or above $\mathfrak q$. Any chain splits there, and chains in the two intervals concatenate at $\mathfrak q$. Their maximal lengths therefore add, giving $\operatorname{ht}(W)=\operatorname{ht}(A)+\operatorname{ht}(W/\mathfrak q)$. These lengths are finite by Step 2; the same interval argument applies to any finite-height valuation ring and its overring.

source.place: Composition discussion before Lemma 2.1.4: the two spectra are glued at the closed/generic point; localization prime correspondence is Stacks Tag 00E3, algebra-lemma-spec-localization.

proof.text: Now assume $h>0$ and $(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}W=L$. The finite height bound and total ordering of primes from Step 4 imply that $W$ has finitely many primes: otherwise a selection of $h+d+2$ distinct primes gives a chain longer than $h+d$. Also $W\ne L$, since $W=L$ would give $R=K$, of height zero. Its maximal ideal is therefore nonzero. Choose the least nonzero prime $\mathfrak q$ and set $A=W_{\mathfrak q}$, the valuation overring supplied by [lem-trf-valuation-overring-prime-localization]. The localization prime correspondence gives exactly two primes in $A$, namely zero and its nonzero maximal ideal, so its height is one. Step 3 identifies that maximal ideal as the same subset $\mathfrak q\subseteq W$. Put $R_1=A\cap K$; it is a valuation ring by the element/inverse alternative. If $R_1=K$, then $A$ contains every inverse of an element of $R\setminus\{0\}$, hence contains $(R\setminus\{0\})^{-1}W=L$, contradicting its height one. Thus $R_1\ne K$.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 2.1.8, printed p. 13, choosing the induced height-one valuations after the boundedness reduction; explicit minimal-prime construction.

proof.text: To see that $R_1$ has height one, embed $H_1=K^\times/R_1^\times$ as an ordered subgroup of $\Gamma_1=L^\times/A^\times$ by ratios as in Step 2. By [lem-trf-valuation-prime-convex-correspondence] for $A$, the only convex subgroups of $\Gamma_1$ are zero and $\Gamma_1$. For $c>0$, the subgroup $C_c=\{g:|g|\le nc\text{ for some integer }n\ge0\}$ is convex (addition uses $(n+m)c$, inverses preserve absolute value). Thus $C_c=\Gamma_1$. Any nonzero convex subgroup $D$ of $H_1$ contains some $c>0$, so for every $x\in H_1$ we have $|x|\le nc$ and hence $x\in D$. There are therefore at most two convex subgroups of $H_1$. Applying the prime/convex correspondence to $R_1$ bounds its height by one; Step 5 proved it is not a field, so its height is exactly one.

source.place: Section 2.1, ordered value groups and prime/convex correspondence; height-one restriction is written out using principal convex subgroups.

proof.text: Put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap K$. It is the maximal ideal of $R_1$, since an element of $R_1$ is a unit exactly when both it and its inverse are in $A\cap K$. Also $\mathfrak p\subseteq R$ by Step 3. Apply the quotient and inverse-image argument of Step 3 to $R\subseteq R_1$, and the height addition of Step 4 to this pair. We obtain that $R_0=R/\mathfrak p$ is a valuation ring of $k=R_1/\mathfrak p$ and $\operatorname{ht}(R_0)=h-1$. Similarly $W_0=W/\mathfrak q$ is a valuation ring of $E=A/\mathfrak q$. The inclusion $R_1\subseteq A$ induces the embedding $k\subseteq E$, with kernel $\mathfrak p$. If a class from $k$ belongs to $W_0$, choose representatives $r\in R_1$ and $w\in W$ with $r-w\in\mathfrak q$. Then $\mathfrak q\subseteq W$ gives $r\in W\cap K=R$. Conversely every class from $R$ belongs to both rings. Hence $W_0\cap k=R_0$, proving compatibility of both the coarse and residual valuations.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.4(i) and the height-induction paragraph of Theorem 2.1.8, p. 13; explicit residue intersection.

proof.text: Finally let $K\subseteq F\subseteq L$. Set $A_F=A\cap F$, $W_F=W\cap F$ and $\mathfrak q_F=\mathfrak q\cap F$. The element/inverse alternative makes both restricted rings valuation rings, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak q_F$ for $A_F$. The induced map $A_F/\mathfrak q_F\to A/\mathfrak q$ is injective because its kernel on $A_F$ is $\mathfrak q_F$. Under this embedding, $(W/\mathfrak q)\cap(A_F/\mathfrak q_F)=W_F/\mathfrak q_F$: for the reverse inclusion lift a common class to $a\in A_F$ and $w\in W$; $a-w\in\mathfrak q\subseteq W$ gives $a\in W_F$. Thus an $a\in A_F$ has residue in $W_F/\mathfrak q_F$ if and only if $a\in W_F$. This proves that restriction commutes with each inverse-image description, including the original arbitrary overring in Steps 3–4.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.4(i), applied to subfields; restriction and inverse images checked on residue representatives.
